questions.explanation: Without virtual inheritance, a `Bottom` contains two distinct `Top` subobjects, one through `Left` and one through `Right`. The derived-to-base conversion must identify a unique subobject, so it is ill-formed. There is no rule preferring the first base; write `static_cast<Left*>(&b)` first, or make `Top` a virtual base.

The most derived class constructs its virtual bases first, before any non-virtual base, so the single shared `V` comes before `N` even though `N` is listed first. Then the direct bases run in declaration order, `N`, `L`, `R`, and finally the body of `M`. `V` appears once because both paths share one virtual base subobject, which rules out the options with two `V` lines.

It finds `put` in two different base class subobjects, so the lookup result is ambiguous and the program is ill-formed, whatever the argument types. The first option is how people expect overloading to work; it does once `Device` declares `using Reader::put; using Writer::put;`.

questions.explanation: A virtual base is initialized by the most derived class, here `Bottom`, using its mem-initializer `Top(3)`. The mem-initializers `Top(1)` in `Left` and `Top(2)` in `Right` are ignored because those constructors are not running for the most derived object. `Top 1` is the tempting answer for anyone who expects the first base on the path to win.

questions.explanation: `reinterpret_cast` between object pointers behaves like `static_cast` through `void*`, and that only lands on a different object when the two are pointer-interconvertible. A class is not pointer-interconvertible with its second base, so `p` still points at the `B` subobject, and accessing `p->c` as if it were a `C` is undefined behavior. `static_cast<C*>(pb)` would subtract the base offset and print 3, which is why the first option is tempting. The cast itself compiles.

Because `Top` is a virtual base, the `Top` subobject seen through `Right` is the same one that is a base of `Left`, so [class.member.lookup] discards `Top::f` in favour of `Left::f`; this is dominance. If `Top` were a non-virtual base, the two declarations would be in unrelated subobjects and the call would be ambiguous, which is why the third option is tempting.

questions.explanation: [expr.static.cast] allows a downcast from `B*` to `D*` only if `B` is neither a virtual base of `D` nor a base of a virtual base of `D`. The offset from a virtual base to the derived class depends on the most derived object, so a static conversion cannot compute it and B is ill-formed. `dynamic_cast` reads it from the object at run time and is well-formed here. The last option describes downcasting from a non-virtual base.
